title: A precept kept as to substance can still be sin; or it can have a natural moral honesty
source_text: VI. Rursus observant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae illos qui legis praecepta quoad operum substantiam observant, nec tamen istud ex charitate praestant, in duplici adhuc esse differentia. Potest enim, inquiunt, legis aliquod praeceptum servari quoad substantiam operis, etiam cum peccato, & ita ut actio laudabilis vel honesta censeri non debeat. Quum scilicet, aliquis agit ex prava cupiditate, & in malum aliquem finem, ut si quis depositum amico restituat, & largiatur aliquid egenti, sed in gratiam meretricis, & ut affectui impudico serviat. Sed quamvis aliquis Dei charitate non ducatur, potest aliquod praeceptum quoad substantiam operis servare, non ex prava cupiditate, sed ex affectu naturali non malo, & finem malum non intendens: seu quia existimat id esse sui officii, & rationi congruum: ita ut in eo novum peccatum non incurrat, sed opus quod ab eo praestatur, moralem quandam honestatem habeat. Ac in ejusmodi mandatorum legis observatione consistit illud bonum quod Scholastici morale appellant, & opponunt bono non tantum naturali, sed etiam supernaturali.
pass_a_gloss: VI. Again the Doctors of the Roman Church observe that those who observe the precepts of the law as to the substance of the works, and yet do not perform it from charity, are still in a twofold difference. For, they say, some precept of the law can be kept as to the substance of the work even with sin, and so that the action ought not to be judged praiseworthy or honest. Namely when someone acts from depraved desire, and toward some evil end, as if someone restores a deposit to a friend, and gives something to the needy, but to win favour with a harlot, and to serve an unchaste affection. But although someone is not led by the charity of God, he can keep some precept as to the substance of the work, not from depraved desire, but from a natural affection not evil, and not intending an evil end: or because he judges it to be of his duty, and agreeable to reason: so that in it he does not incur a new sin, but the work which is performed by him has a certain moral honesty. And in the observance of the commandments of the law of this kind consists that good which the Scholastics call moral, and oppose to good not only natural, but also supernatural.
pass_b_english: The doctors of the Roman Church further observe that those who keep the precepts as to the substance of the works, but not out of charity, still fall into two classes.

'A precept of the law,' they say, 'can be kept as to the substance of the work and still be kept with sin, so that the act should not be counted praiseworthy or honourable. This happens when someone acts from a corrupt desire and for a bad end: for instance, if he returns a deposit to a friend or gives something to the needy, but to please a harlot and serve an unchaste passion.

But a man who is not moved by the love of God can still keep a precept as to the substance of the work, not from corrupt desire but from a natural affection that is not evil, and without aiming at a bad end, because he thinks it his duty and agreeable to reason. Then he commits no new sin in doing it, and the work he does has a certain moral honesty.' The good the Schoolmen call moral consists in keeping the commandments in this way, and they set it against both natural and supernatural good.

choices.why: The scholastic distinction between doing what a precept requires and doing it in the manner that orders it to salvation; kept as the technical phrase.
